title: Stripping STRIPs Trading Activity - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed researchers Fleming and Shachar publish the first detailed breakdown of Treasury STRIPS trading from FINRA TRACE: $560 billion outstanding (2.5 percent of marketable coupon debt), $5.6 billion of daily volume against $739 billion for coupon Treasuries, with 98.1 percent of stripped stock in long bonds and 68 percent of volume in principal STRIPS. Activity is overwhelmingly dealer-to-client (88 percent for principal STRIPS) in large clips that grow with maturity, evidencing liability-driven pension and insurer demand for long duration, while trade counts peak in the 0-5 year bucket.

insights.claim: As of end-June 2025, $560 billion of U.S. Treasury securities were held in stripped (zero-coupon) form, just 2.5 percent of the $22.2 trillion in marketable notes, bonds, and TIPS outstanding.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of the zero-coupon Treasury complex: small relative to the overall market, so STRIPS flows are a niche but concentrated source of long-duration demand rather than a driver of aggregate Treasury supply.
insights.quote: As of the end of June 2025, $560 billion in U.S. Treasury securities were held in stripped form, accounting for 2.5 percent of the $22.2 trillion in marketable notes, bonds
insights.locator: Which Securities are Stripped?

insights.claim: Stripping is overwhelmingly a long-bond phenomenon: bonds account for 98.1 percent of Treasuries held in stripped form, notes 1.9 percent, and TIPS just 0.002 percent, while bills and floating rate notes are ineligible for stripping.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Zero-coupon demand is almost entirely a bid for 20-30 year duration; watch the long end, not the belly, for STRIPS-driven flow effects.
insights.quote: bonds account for 98.1 percent of Treasuries held in stripped form, notes 1.9 percent, and (TIPS) 0.002 percent
insights.locator: Which Securities are Stripped?

insights.claim: Stripping intensity varies enormously across individual Treasury bonds: the bond maturing on May 15, 2053 was 36 percent stripped, the most of any Treasury security, while the most recently issued bond in the 25-30 year sector was only 7 percent stripped.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Security-level stripping percentages flag where liability-driven demand has locked up float; heavily stripped CUSIPs have less freely circulating collateral, a candidate explanation for individual-issue richness and repo specialness.
insights.quote: the bond maturing on May 15, 2053 was 36 percent stripped, the most of any Treasury security
insights.locator: The prevalence of stripped securities by sector

insights.claim: Original 20-year Treasury bonds show markedly weaker stripping demand than 30-year bonds, with six issues in the 15-20 year maturity sector carrying no stripped amount at all.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Adds a structural-demand explanation for the persistent cheapness of the 20-year point: liability-driven buyers are not stripping it, so it lacks the zero-coupon bid that supports 30-year issues.
insights.quote: In the 15-20 year sector, six bonds were not stripped at all, all of which were originally issued as 20-year bonds.
insights.locator: In the 15-20 year sector, six bonds

insights.claim: Between July 2024 and June 2025, an average of $1,827 million of Treasuries were stripped each day while $1,567 million were reconstituted, leaving net stripping of roughly $260 million per day.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Gross two-way flow dwarfs the net change, meaning stripping is an active arbitrage channel rather than one-way accumulation; the gross numbers are the ones to watch for dislocation.
insights.quote: on average, $1,827 million in Treasuries were stripped each day from July 2024 to June 2025 and $1,567 million reconstituted
insights.locator: The flow of securities stripped by sector

insights.claim: Reconstitution of a stripped Treasury occurs when demand pushes the whole security's price above the summed price of its individual stripped components, making stripping and reconstitution a price-driven arbitrage loop between coupon bonds and zeros.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: A clean mental model for long-end relative value: the strip/reconstitute boundary caps how far zero-coupon curve pricing can diverge from coupon-bond pricing.
insights.quote: Reconstitution may occur because demand for a reconstituted security increases its price above that of its stripped components.
insights.locator: Note that components of a stripped Treasury

insights.claim: The daily flow of Treasuries being stripped by maturity sector is highly correlated with the existing stock of stripped securities, with both stripping and reconstitution concentrated in the long end of the curve.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Flow follows stock, so the long-end concentration of zero-coupon demand is structurally persistent rather than a transient positioning artifact.
insights.locator: The flow of securities stripped by sector

insights.claim: Zero-coupon Treasury STRIPS traded an average of $5.6 billion per day from July 2024 to June 2025, versus $739 billion per day for Treasury notes, bonds, and TIPS — under 1 percent of coupon Treasury turnover.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Quantifies how thin the zero-coupon market is relative to coupon Treasuries: liquidity, not availability, is the binding size constraint for anyone expressing duration views through STRIPS.
insights.quote: Treasury notes, bonds, and TIPS traded $739 billion per day on average from July 2024 to June 2025
insights.locator: How Much Do STRIPS Trade?

insights.claim: Principal STRIPS account for 68 percent ($3,856 million per day) of STRIPS trading volume versus 32 percent ($1,784 million) for coupon STRIPS, even though stripping a 10-year note creates twenty coupon STRIPS for every single principal STRIPS.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Turnover per outstanding security is dramatically higher in principal STRIPS — that is where tradable liquidity sits, and a likely source of the documented principal-versus-coupon STRIPS price premium.
insights.quote: Daily trading volume of STRIPS averaged $5.6 billion from July 2024 to June 2025, with coupon STRIPS accounting for 32 percent ($1,784 million) and principal STRIPS 68 percent ($3,856 million).
insights.locator: How Much Do STRIPS Trade?

insights.claim: Coupon STRIPS trading volume is spread relatively evenly across maturity buckets while principal STRIPS volume concentrates in long maturities, because stripping generates semi-annual coupon STRIPS across the whole horizon but only one principal STRIPS at final maturity.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: The maturity distribution of STRIPS supply is mechanically set by the stripping process, so the even spread of coupon STRIPS activity is partly a supply artifact and should not be read as investor preference.
insights.quote: the stripping process creates semi-annual coupon STRIPS from the present to the stripped security’s final maturity, but principal STRIPS with only the stripped security’s final maturity
insights.locator: Consistent with stripping activity

insights.claim: About 73 percent of coupon STRIPS daily volume trades dealer-to-client ($1,309 million), 19 percent dealer-to-dealer ($338 million), and only 8 percent through interdealer brokers ($137 million).
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Interdealer STRIPS liquidity is tiny, so dealers warehousing client zero-coupon risk have little ability to lay it off quickly — a latent capacity constraint in long-duration risk transfer.
insights.locator: Breaking down trading activity by venue

insights.claim: Principal STRIPS are even more client-driven than coupon STRIPS, with 88 percent of daily volume ($3,396 million) transacted in the dealer-to-client segment.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Nearly all long-duration zero-coupon activity is end-user flow crossing dealer balance sheets rather than dealer risk recycling, making dealer capacity the chokepoint if pension or insurer demand surges.
insights.quote: The volumes of principal STRIPS are even more concentrated in the DTC segment with 88 percent of daily volume (averaging $3,396 million).
insights.locator: Breaking down trading activity by venue

insights.claim: The heavy dealer-to-client share of zero-coupon Treasury trading likely reflects the value that end-users such as pension funds and insurance companies place on single-payment securities they can match directly against dated liabilities.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: STRIPS volume is a proxy for liability-driven investor duration demand; sustained pickups in dealer-to-client principal STRIPS volume would signal pension and insurer hedging at the long end.
insights.quote: The high share of DTC activity likely reflects the value that end-users such as pension funds and insurance companies ascribe to these single-payment securities.
insights.locator: Breaking down trading activity by venue

insights.claim: Principal STRIPS trade in average sizes of about $7 million versus roughly $850 thousand for coupon STRIPS, with dealer-to-client principal STRIPS trades averaging $10.47 million against $1.09 million through interdealer brokers.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Block-size zero-coupon trades are executed bilaterally with dealers, confirming institutional-size long-duration risk cannot be moved on interdealer venues.
insights.quote: Coupon STRIPS trade with an average size of about $850 thousand, whereas principal STRIPS trade with an average trade size of about $7 million.
insights.locator: The coupon vs. principal STRIPS activity gap

insights.claim: Average principal STRIPS trade size in the 25-30 year sector is about $12.3 million, roughly 4 times the $2.8 million average in the 10-15 year sector, while coupon STRIPS trade sizes scale only about 2.5 times ($2.5 million vs. $1.0 million) across the same range.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Ticket size rises with duration, so the longest-dated principal STRIPS are where the largest single-clip institutional duration transfers occur — the cleanest place to observe real-money long-end demand.
insights.quote: Trade sizes in the 25-30 year sector are thus about 4 times larger than those in the 10-15 year sector for principal STRIPS ($12.3 million vs. $2.8 million)
insights.locator: Longer maturity STRIPS also trade

insights.claim: The 0-5 year maturity bucket is the most frequently traded STRIPS sector by number of trades, with roughly equal numbers of dealer-to-client and dealer-to-dealer trades each day, despite holding little of the stripped stock.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Trade count and notional volume point in opposite directions across the curve — short-dated zeros trade in many small tickets, so headline volume alone misreads who uses which part of the curve.
insights.quote: Interestingly, the 0-5 year maturity bucket is most frequently traded, with roughly the same number of DTC and DTD trades each trading day.
insights.locator: Lastly, we explore trading frequency

insights.claim: Trade frequency for principal STRIPS is U-shaped across the curve — declining out to the 10-15 year bucket then rising again for longer maturities — whereas coupon STRIPS trade frequency declines monotonically as maturity extends.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Two distinct clienteles are visible: short-dated tactical users and long-dated liability hedgers, leaving the 10-15 year zero-coupon sector the least active and likely least liquid.
insights.quote: for principal STRIPS the average daily number of trades first decreases but then increases as securities’ maturities extend beyond 10-15 years
insights.locator: Lastly, we explore trading frequency

themes.theme: Transparency gap and open pricing question

insights.claim: FINRA has published aggregate Treasury trading volume since March 2020 but its public data exclude STRIPS entirely, making this TRACE-based study the first detailed analysis of zero-coupon Treasury trading activity.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: A genuine transparency blind spot in a $560 billion segment; any move to publish STRIPS volumes would give the market a currently unavailable read on liability-driven duration demand.
insights.quote: The public data do not, however, include information about the trading activity of Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities (STRIPS).
insights.locator: In March 2020, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority

insights.claim: Principal STRIPS consistently trade at higher prices than coupon STRIPS of the same maturity, and the authors flag as unresolved whether their higher trading volume translates into higher liquidity that explains the pricing gap.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: A concrete relative-value hypothesis: if the principal-STRIPS premium is a liquidity premium rather than structural, matched-maturity coupon STRIPS are the cheaper way to buy identical government cash flows for buy-and-hold liability matching.
insights.quote: the extent to which the higher trading volume of principal STRIPS is associated with higher liquidity and whether liquidity differences in the STRIPS market can help explain the pricing differences
insights.locator: Summing Up

insights.claim: Each stripped Treasury cash flow gets its own CUSIP while remaining a direct obligation of the U.S. government, giving investors known cash values at specific future dates for exact liability matching, and the high duration of long-maturity zeros also makes them a favored speculative vehicle.
insights.speaker: Michael J. Fleming and Or Shachar
insights.so_what: Explains why long zero-coupon Treasuries are the highest-duration, highest-convexity expression of a rates view available in government paper — leveraged duration with no credit risk.
insights.quote: The flexibility to customize investments, and the high duration of long maturity STRIPS, also make them popular with speculators.
insights.locator: As STRIPS have known cash values
